name: Assamese
variety: Standard colloquial Assamese of eastern (Upper) Assam, Jorhat-Sibsagar, as in Mahanta 2012
sources: Mahanta, Shakuntala (2012). Assamese. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(2), 217-224.
Mahanta, Shakuntala (2008). Directionality and Locality in Vowel Harmony: With Special Reference to Vowel Harmony in Assamese. LOT Dissertation Series 173, Utrecht.
Goswami, Golok Chandra (1966). An Introduction to Assamese Phonology. Poona: Deccan College.
Goswami, Golok Chandra & Tamuli, Jyotiprakash (2003). Asamiya. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Kakati, Banikanta (1962). Assamese, its Formation and Development, 3rd edn. Gauhati: Lawyer's Book Stall.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Ladefoged, Peter & Maddieson, Ian (1996). The Sounds of the World's Languages. Oxford: Blackwell.
Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2016). The intonation of South Asian languages: towards a comparative analysis. Proceedings of Formal Approaches to South Asian Languages 6, 23-36.
contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops at three places (labial, alveolar, velar): voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced
no dental versus retroflex contrast: the two series of the script are one alveolar series
no affricates: the letters for the old palatal stops are /s/ and /z/
voiceless velar fricative /x/, the reflex of the old sibilants (/ɔxɔm/ 'Assam')
eight oral vowels with a three-way back contrast /u/ : /ʊ/ : /o/ : /ɔ/ (/bul/, /bʊl/ 'colour', /bol/ 'let us go', /bɔɹ/ 'big')
oral versus nasal vowels only for /ɑ/ and /ʊ/ (/sɑ/ 'look' : /sɑ̃/ 'shadow')
the rhotic is an alveolar approximant /ɹ/
allophony: regressive tongue-root harmony: /ɛ ɔ ʊ/ become [e o u] when the next syllable has /i/ or /u/ (/pɔlɔx/ 'silt', [poloxuwɑ] 'fertile land'); a nasal next to the trigger or a coda consonant blocks it
[e] and [o] occur almost only through harmony, and in loans
breathy voiced stops lose their breathiness in non-initial position ([bɑɡʱ] > [bɑɡ] 'tiger')
/z/ is [dz] for some speakers in prominent positions and is partly devoiced elsewhere; [zʲ] before /j/
/t tʰ d dʱ n/ are denti-alveolar next to high front vowels and apico-alveolar next to back vowels
/ɹ/ is optionally deleted outside initial position, with lengthening of the preceding vowel ([ɑmɑɹ] ~ [ɑmɑː] 'our')
vowels are long in open syllables and shorter in closed syllables
oral vowels are nasalised after nasal consonants
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C); clusters mainly in Sanskrit and English loans
phonotactics: /ŋ/ does not occur word-initially; /w j/ are restricted
the inherent vowel is /ɔ/ (or [o] by harmony); final inherent vowels are mostly dropped after single consonants and kept after clusters
consonant gemination occurs in the standard variety (/uttɔɹ/ 'answer', /unnois/ 'nineteen')
the letters for sibilants are /x/, and [s] in some clusters

stress.type: weight-sensitive within the first two syllables, weak, not contrastive
stress.rule: Prominence falls on the first syllable, unless the first is open and the second is closed, in which case it falls on the second; never later (Mahanta 2001, cited in Mahanta 2012).
stress.cues: a low pitch that rises towards the end of the prominent syllable; duration and intensity are not used

rhythm.notes: Class and final lengthening are assumptions from the areal pattern; no measurement could be verified.

length.notes: No phonemic vowel length; vowels are phonetically longer in open syllables. Geminates occur but their duration has not been measured in a source I can name; central dialects degeminate.

intonation.declarative: a chain of rising phrases, one per content word with its clitics: low on the first syllable, high at the right edge (L* ... H); the last phrase falls to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: rising phrases and a high final boundary
intonation.wh_question: as a declarative, low final boundary
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases; low-rising boundary at clause ends
intonation.accent_shape: L* ... H: low on the word-initial syllable (the low target can shift rightwards), peak on the last syllable of the phrase
intonation.notes: From Khan 2016, which reports the analysis of Twaha & Mahanta and the recording of Mahanta 2012. Sentence-type boundary tones are given as the typical South Asian pattern, not from an Assamese study I can cite directly.

phonation: breathy voiced stops /bʱ dʱ ɡʱ/, fully breathy only word-initially

problems: Only the letter স gives a fricative of the /x/ type, and it is the uvular [χ] followed by a schwa (অসম [ɔχəm]); শ and ষ are [ʃ], a sound Assamese does not have (শেষ [ʃeʃ] for [xɛx]).
চ and ছ are both the affricate [tʃ] (চাহ [tʃaho]); Assamese has /s/. জ is the palatal stop [ɟ] and য is [dʒ]; Assamese has /z/.
Dental and retroflex stops are kept apart (ত [t̪] : ট [ʈ]) although Assamese has a single alveolar series.
ৰ is the tap [ɾ] of the Hindi base table, not the approximant [ɹ].
There is no /ʊ/: ও is [o], the apostrophe that marks /o/ in ক'লা is ignored, and harmony is applied only to the first inherent vowel.
Word-final হ and ত receive an extra [o] (মানুহ [manuho], ভাত [bʰato], দাঁত [dãto]).
ৱ before a vowel sign inserts [ɔ] (ৱাহ [wɔaho]).

The decomposed form of য় (U+09AF U+09BC, which is what Unicode normalisation produces) is not in the rules, so words containing it are spelled out letter by letter; the precomposed ড় (U+09DC) switches to the Bengali voice.
Breathy voiced stops and h come from the Hindi base table (voiced closure plus voiceless aspiration sample); intonation uses the generic tunes.
good: the inherent vowel is [o] before /i u/ in the next syllable, for the first syllable

notes: Mahanta 2012 counts only /ɑ̃/ and /ʊ̃/ as phonemic nasal vowels; other descriptions allow nasalisation of most vowels. Ladefoged & Maddieson describe the vowel written ʊ here as a low back vowel with strong rounding; Mahanta argues for /ʊ/. [f ʃ dʒ] occur only in unassimilated loans. No formant table could be verified, so vowel_formants is left out.
